Alex / CivicTech team,

Thanks for returning the redlined order form. I reviewed the high-level ask and wanted to call out two items that will need coordination with legal: governing law / forum selection and the carveout for injunctive relief. Attaching your redlines and our preferred language for context. (See attachments: CivicTech_OrderForm_Redlines_v2.pdf; redwood_preferred_dispute_language.docx).

Quick summary of the positions I’m seeing:
- CivicTech prefers California courts (SF) and has limited the arbitration carveout.
- You also propose restricting equitable relief language in a way that would make emergency injunctive access more difficult.

We usually ask for Delaware law for our commercial contracts, with arbitration for most disputes and a narrow exception allowing courts to provide injunctive/temporary equitable relief to preserve rights (IP, data protection, injunctive relief to stop misuse of models, etc.). I don’t expect CivicTech to accept Delaware flat-out without some give, so I’m proposing Legal consider a compromise: Delaware law; arbitration as the default forum; explicit, narrowly tailored carveout permitting interim injunctive relief in a convenient US federal or state court for enforcement (e.g., Northern District of California) for issues involving IP, data security, or misuse.

Can you and Legal weigh in on whether the carveout below is negotiable (and whether the language below is acceptable to send back as a proposal)? If so I’ll propose it to CivicTech and loop Ben on commercial tradeoffs.

Proposed carveout (draft, not final):
"Notwithstanding the agreement to arbitrate, either party may seek temporary injunctive or other interim equitable relief in a court of competent jurisdiction to protect confidential information, intellectual property, or prevent the unauthorized use or disclosure of Customer Data. Such court proceedings shall not constitute a waiver of the obligation to arbitrate other claims, and the parties agree that, for the limited purpose of seeking such relief, venue may be proper in the federal or state courts located in the Northern District of California or the State of Delaware, depending on the nature of the request and the party seeking relief."

If Legal wants different venue language or prefers a single seat, flag that. I’ll await direction before circling back to CivicTech.

Thanks,
Vanessa Ortiz
Enterprise Account Executive
Redwood Inference

Vanessa — thanks for the summary and the suggested carveout. A few thoughts from our side:

- CivicTech cannot agree to Delaware as the governing law for this order form. We need a forum that gives our team predictable local process and enforcement — SF/California is our preference.
- We are generally open to arbitration for substantive claims, but we are uncomfortable with language that lets Redwood unilaterally choose Delaware as the governing law while limiting CivicTech’s access to local courts for urgent relief.
- We are willing to accept a narrow injunctive-relief carveout limited to intellectual property and data protection, but we would prefer the carveout to specify that such relief may be sought in California state or federal courts (we can accept Northern District of California for federal).

If you can accept California courts for enforcement of injunctive relief and keep substantive law as California for the order form, we can probably move forward. Alternately, if Redwood insists on Delaware law, we would ask for a clear waiver that allows us to seek temporary relief in California courts without prejudice to arbitration.

We’ve attached our redline to show the exact language we changed. Happy to hop on a 20–30 minute call if that speeds this up.

Best,
Alex Gomez

Vanessa / Ben / Aditya —

Thanks for the context. I reviewed CivicTech's redlines and drafted two short options below with pros/cons. I also attached a redline file with exact language (Redwood_MS_OrderForm_Dispute_Language_redline.docx).

Option A (preferred operationally):
- Governing law: Delaware.
- Dispute resolution: binding arbitration for all substantive disputes.
- Carveout: narrow interim equitable relief carveout permitting either party to seek temporary injunctive relief in the federal or state courts located in the Northern District of California solely for issues related to confidentiality, IP, or unauthorized use of Redwood-hosted models or Customer Data. Any such court action shall be limited to temporary equitable relief pending resolution of the underlying dispute in arbitration.

Pros: preserves our commercial standard (Delaware/arbitration) while giving CivicTech the speed of California courts for emergency relief. Limits forum exposure; keeps main dispute path in arbitration.
Cons: CivicTech may still press for California law; they could argue the availability of CA courts should come with CA substantive law.

Draft clause (Option A):
"Notwithstanding any agreement to arbitrate, either party may seek provisional or injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction to protect its confidential information, intellectual property, or to prevent the unauthorized use or disclosure of Customer Data. Such relief shall be limited to temporary measures pending the outcome of arbitration and shall not be deemed a waiver of the obligation to arbitrate. For purposes of such temporary relief, venue may be proper in the federal or state courts located in the Northern District of California."

Option B (commercial compromise):
- Governing law: California.
- Dispute resolution: arbitration remains the primary pathway for substantive disputes; injunctive relief can be sought in California courts.

Pros: easier sell to CivicTech; likely shortens negotiation.
Cons: gives up Delaware law precedent; slightly higher legal risk/cost for Redwood on a per-account basis.

Recommendation: propose Option A to CivicTech first. If CivicTech pushes back strongly on Delaware law, switch to Option B as a concession tied to a modest commercial concession (e.g., a shorter commitment term or pricing credit).

If you want, I can send the redline back to CivicTech with the Option A language and a short note: we can accept Northern District of California for temporary injunctive relief but reserve Delaware law and arbitration for substantive claims. Approve and I’ll send.

Laura Bennett
Senior Counsel, Contracts & Commercial
Redwood Inference
